{{Short description|Geometric shape}}
[[File:Biconcave disc.svg|thumb|A biconcave disc]]
In geometry and [[mathematical biology]], a '''biconcave disc''' — also referred to as a '''discocyte'''<ref name="kuchelfackerell">{{Cite journal |last1=Kuchel |first1=Philip W. |last2=Fackerell |first2=Edward D. |year=1999 |title=Parametric-equation representation of biconcave erythrocytes |journal=Bulletin of Mathematical Biology |language=en |volume=61 |issue=2 |pages=209–220 |doi=10.1006/bulm.1998.0064 |pmid=17883208 |s2cid=39585695 |issn=1522-9602 }}</ref> — is a geometric shape resembling an [[oblate spheroid]] with two [[wikt:concavity|concavities]] on the top and on the bottom.

Biconcave discs appear in the study of [[cell biology]], as an approximation to the shape of certain cells, including [[red blood cell]]s.

==Mathematical model==

A biconcave disc can be described mathematically by
:<math>z(r) = D \sqrt{1 - \frac{4r^2}{D^2}} \left(a_0 + \frac{a_1 r^2}{D^2} + \frac{a_2 r^4}{D^4} \right)</math>
where {{math|z(r)}} is the height of the surface as a function of radius {{math|r}}, {{math|D}} is the diameter of the disc, and {{math|a<sub>0</sub>, a<sub>1</sub>, a<sub>2</sub>}} are coefficients describing the shape.  The above model describes a smooth surface; actual cells can be much more irregular.

==Biology==
[[Erythrocytes]], also known as red blood cells that transport oxygen to and from tissues, are in the shape of a biconcave disc.<ref name="kuchelfackerell" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Muñoz |first1=Sagrario |last2=Sebastián |first2=José L. |last3=Sancho |first3=Miguel F. |last4=Álvarez |first4=Gabriel |date=2014-03-01 |title=Elastic energy of the discocyte–stomatocyte transformation |journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Biomembranes |volume=1838 |issue=3 |pages=950–956 |doi=10.1016/j.bbamem.2013.10.020 |pmid=24192054 |issn=0005-2736 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Research findings state that owing to the [[turbulent flow]] in the [[cardiovascular system]], the human erythrocytes adopt a biconcave disc shape to maximise [[laminar flow]] and minimise [[platelet]] scatter. The biconcave shape has more mass distributed on the periphery which increases its moment of inertia and makes the cell less prone to rotation during flow which promotes laminar flow and reduces platelet scattering by minimising "Eddy currents" and thus, also suppresses [[atherogenic]] activity in the large vessels.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Abstract : The human erythrocyte has developed the biconcave disc shape to optimise the flow properties of the blood in the large vessels |url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16797867/}}</ref>
